text: I found a problem with your circuit. If we fed an audio signal with a DC offset, which is very likely to happen, our amp would clip out most of our wave and a lot of distortion would occur. You can add a .1uF cap series to the audio signal. Another thing is that you are using only one channel of the stereo plug. You can combine the two channels with two 1K resistors to create mono out of it. A summing amplifier and a differential amplifier could also be used in order to make an "analog or gate" or basically adding the signals on top of each other, that would be a neater solution. It would be nice to add a 10K pullup resistor before the cap in order to power electret microphones. The dc offset will be filtered by the cap.

text:
Pin 3 is correct. The capacitor is intended to short radio frequencies immisions from the non-inverting input to ground. But in the video is another more relevant error. The positive electrode of the output capacitor (1000 µF) is not connected to pin 5 (output) of the LM386 but to the midpoint of the Zobel circuit. So the speaker will only get less than half of the voltage and less than a quarter of the power.
 
And the Zobel circuit is connected with the resistor to the output of the LM386 and with the capacitor to the ground (the opposite as in the tutorial). It doesn't matter the way it is but if it would have been built in the way like in the tutorial, the educator would have realized that the output capacitor is at the wrong net, because only the very high frequencies would have been audible. :D

text:
Generally speaking in audio applications, gain is a multiplier for amps (opamps etc) and can be controlled using the negative feedback of the amp. For example if I had a 3v sine wave peak to peak on the input of the amp and have a gain of 2, then my final signal will be 6v peak to peak. 

Volume is a final "fine tuning" of the loudness. It's simply a voltage divider at the end of a signal usually controlled by a potentiometer. 

A (very basic) example of them being used together would be in a basic distortion circuit for a guitar. Guitar signal is fed to the op amp which has a gain higher than what the amp can produce. The result is distortion; however, your signal becomes really loud to create this distortion. So you add a volume control at the end of the of the circuit to tame the loud signal

text:
The circuit does work, but as I mentioned in the video, there may be some noise due to loose connections from using a breadboard. It would also help to use wires as short as possible to prevent electromagnetic interference. Also try to make sure the wires are as close as possible to the LM386. And using capacitors with smaller tolerance should help as well. Keep in mind that this is not a HiFi Amp, but it does sound good. For the best audio quality i'd look into building a tube amp

The green capacitors are polyester film capacitors
